title: A filter and a choice
header_line: My analysis of one book on an entrepreneur's life. Not a summary of the book. Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.

lines.text: How would you test whether someone really wants to be on your team?
I asked what we can learn from the mentality behind the cuts. A student said: he did not want anyone who was not hardcore or extraordinary.

I described a story from the book: staff who had made a big effort to come into the office were kept waiting, hungry, for hours. I asked why it might be on purpose, and said: as a filter. It tests people's ability to handle adversity.
A student said: when he had people opt in instead of opt out.
I said: what a great filter that is.
By giving them a choice, I said, he removes the responsibility from himself and shifts it to them. You are making a decision. This is the choice you are making.
I said that many people will say: he's the boss, he pays me. A million things can get in the way of a true answer, so the question is whether they say: I really believe in it, I'm in, I'm opting in.

A student said: if you give someone the alternative, not as a trap, you will read their answer or they will give you an honest one. I said that is difficult, because people often do not give you honest answers.
What choice could you put in front of your team so the answer is honest?

exercise.title: Five minutes
steps: Write what you want from the people on your team.
Write a filter you could use that tests it.
Write a choice you could offer that moves the weight to them.
Write why people may not answer honestly.
Write how you would make it safe to answer honestly.

check.q: What did I call the long wait in the story?
What does giving people a choice do, according to me?
What did a student say about giving someone the alternative?
choices: Not as a trap, you get their honest answer

recap: A filter shows who is in. A choice moves the weight to them.
